prompt: Why did Paula never raise the reminder-service problem again after Renata said she would “think about” it?
hint: Five weeks with nothing beside the line.

choices.text: She had solved it herself by documenting the service over a weekend
choices.why: Nothing says so; the problem was still there when Renata noticed.

choices.text: She had decided the problem was not important after all
choices.why: She raised it four times in eight weeks before going quiet; it mattered to her.

choices.text: The silence had answered her
choices.why: Right: with no date and no first step, nothing happened, and the absence told Paula what she needed to know.

choices.text: Renata had asked her not to bring it up again until the quarter planning in eight weeks
choices.why: Renata had promised to think about it; she never asked Paula to stay quiet.

prompt: Match each unkeepable promise with its keepable version from the lesson’s table.
hint: An action, a date, and a report back.

pairs.right: “I’ll get a runbook page written for that alert by Friday”

pairs.left: “I’ll see what I can do about on-call”
pairs.right: “I’ll ask the platform team about a second rota and tell you on Thursday”
“I’ll talk to Otávio about the budget this week and come back either way”

prompt: Why can “I’ll find out and tell you” always be kept, while “I’ll get you the budget” cannot?

choices.text: Budgets are never approved
choices.why: Some are; the point is that approval is not the manager’s to promise.

choices.text: The first is vaguer
choices.why: It is more precise about what the manager will do, which is why it can be kept.

choices.text: Because promises about money need HR’s approval at most companies, and Caju is no exception
choices.why: No such rule appears; the reason is who decides.

choices.text: The first depends only on the manager; the budget is somebody else’s decision
choices.why: Right: when the outcome is out of your hands, promise the report back, not the result.

prompt: Before promising anything, what does the lesson suggest asking?

choices.text: “How urgent is this?”
choices.why: Urgency matters later; the first question is whether action is wanted at all.

choices.text: “Do you want me to do something, or did you want to tell me?”
choices.why: Right: often the person wanted to be heard, and a promise would be a debt nobody asked for.

choices.text: “Who else knows?”
choices.why: Not the lesson’s question.

choices.text: “Can you write it up so I can forward it?”
choices.why: That pushes work back onto the person, which the lesson does not suggest.

prompt: A line on Renata’s promise list is stuck: the platform team will not decide on a second rota for a month. What does the lesson say she does?
hint: A promise you cannot keep can still be closed.

choices.text: Wait until the platform team decides, then report the result
choices.why: A month of silence looks exactly like a dropped promise from the person’s side.

choices.text: Remove the line from the list so it does not distract her during her twice-weekly review
choices.why: Removing it without telling the person is the silent drop the lesson says cannot be closed.

choices.text: Set up the second rota herself
choices.why: The rota is the platform team’s decision; going around them is not in the lesson.

choices.text: Message the person that day, saying it is stuck and why
choices.why: Right: telling the person closes the promise honestly even though the result is not there.

prompt: Which of the three outcomes does the lesson say is most often skipped when closing a loop?

choices.text: It was done
choices.why: Right: the manager assumes the person will notice, and the person may not connect the change with what they said.

choices.text: It is still happening, with a date for the next report
choices.why: That one needs saying, but the lesson singles out the first as the one skipped.

choices.text: The answer is no
choices.why: Managers avoid that one most, which is a different claim from being skipped because it seems obvious.

choices.text: It was forgotten by the manager
choices.why: Not one of the three outcomes, though it happens.

prompt: Put the four parts of Renata’s no to Paula in order.
trap: Opening with the reason or an apology buries the answer, and the person spends the conversation guessing.

prompt: Renata argued for yes, and Otávio said no. How does the lesson say she delivers it?
hint: Whose answer is it, in front of the team?

choices.text: As the team’s answer, without hinting that she disagreed
choices.why: Right: blaming Otávio would undermine the decision and her place in the middle.

choices.text: As Otávio’s decision, so that Paula knows Renata was on her side
choices.why: That is the blame the lesson says she avoided.

choices.text: Softened into a maybe
choices.why: The lesson says she did not soften it, because a maybe keeps the person waiting.

choices.text: By message, to avoid the conversation
choices.why: She told Paula in the one-to-one, in four parts.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a clear no is better than silence?
hint: What can the person do after each?

choices.text: Because a no can always be turned into a yes later, if the manager keeps arguing upwards for long enough
choices.why: A no can be revisited, but that is not why it beats silence.

choices.text: Silence is against company policy
choices.why: No policy is involved.

choices.text: People prefer bad news to good news
choices.why: Nobody prefers bad news; they prefer knowing.

choices.text: It lets the person stop waiting
choices.why: Right: with a no they can make their own decisions; silence keeps them waiting for something that is not coming.

prompt: Which of these close a loop, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Fixing it quietly and saying nothing
choices.why: No: the person may never connect the change to what they raised.

choices.text: “I’m on it.”
choices.why: No: it says nothing about what happened or when.

choices.text: “We dropped the second half of planning, as you suggested.”
choices.why: Yes: the loop running the other way, for an opinion asked for.

choices.text: “The runbook page is up, and Yara is your backup for two weeks.”
choices.why: Yes: done, and what changed.

choices.text: “They discuss it on Tuesday; I’ll tell you on Wednesday.”
choices.why: Yes: still happening, visibly.

prompt: What did reading a quarter of one-to-one notes together reveal that no single meeting showed?

choices.text: Diego was frustrated with design reviews
choices.why: That was vivid and raised once; the tally showed it was not a pattern.

choices.text: On-call was getting worse
choices.why: It was getting better: four mentions in month one, one in month three.

choices.text: Everybody wanted promotion
choices.why: Growth came up for four people, which is not the same thing.

choices.text: Payments was the team’s largest single drag
choices.why: Right: each person treated it as one irritation among several; together it was the biggest.

prompt: In the tally, on-call came up for four people in month one and one person in month three. By how many people did it fall?
Why does the lesson say themes need counting rather than remembering?

choices.text: Counting is required for the quarterly report that goes to Otávio and the rest of leadership
choices.why: Nothing says the tally is reported upwards; it is Renata’s instrument.

choices.text: Memory is always wrong
choices.why: Memory is not always wrong; it is biased towards the vivid.

choices.text: Without a count, the loud wins over the repeated
choices.why: Right: Diego’s vivid complaint was raised once, Paula’s calm sentence four times, and memory favours the first.

choices.text: Themes that are not counted disappear from the notes
choices.why: They stay in the notes; nobody reads them together.

prompt: Otávio’s skip-level meetings surface something that never appeared in Renata’s own notes. How does the lesson read that?
hint: A second instrument, not an audit.

choices.text: Otávio is checking up on her, and she should be careful about what she does next
choices.why: The lesson suggests treating skip-levels as a second instrument rather than an audit.

choices.text: It says something about what people find easy to tell her
choices.why: Right: that is the more useful finding, because it shows a gap in what reaches her.

choices.text: Her notes are wrong and should be rewritten
choices.why: The notes may be accurate about what she was told; the gap is in what she was told.

choices.text: The skip-level is unreliable
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson doubts the skip-level.

prompt: A manager promised a report three weeks ago to “look into” getting them a better laptop. Nothing has happened, and the report has stopped mentioning it. What is the best next step, by this lesson?
hint: Close it, with an outcome and a shape.

choices.text: Tell them what happened, apologise once, and make a dated promise
choices.why: Right: like Renata with Paula, close the silent loop and replace the vague promise with a keepable one.

choices.text: Say nothing, since they have stopped asking
choices.why: Their silence is the answer they drew from his, which is the failure the lesson describes.

choices.text: Order the laptop without telling them
choices.why: They may not connect it to what they asked, and the loop stays open in their mind.

choices.text: Ask them to raise it again in writing
choices.why: That puts the work of the manager’s promise back on the person.
